paper_title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics: the embedding and the unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model's own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model's output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden state of the model readable, attributable and steerable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Between its input and output tokens, language model computes nothing but states of its residual stream, which every layer reads and writes (Elhage et al., 2021). Its vocabulary is in this sense the native semantics of the model, the only units of meaning that it is designed to receive and to express. The model defines the lexical meaning of state at the two ends of the stream: the embedding assigns each token state, and the unembedding maps final state to logits over tokens. Intermediate states lack 1https://github.com/jianguda/lexframe 1 such definition, although interpretability research and its applications read them constantly: early exit and self-speculative decoding stop the computation at layer whose reading already names the output (Schuster et al., 2022; Elhoushi et al., 2024), hallucination detectors judge an answer by its hidden states (Orgad et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), and knowledge editors locate and rewrite facts at intermediate layers (Meng et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2025). Each depends on how faithfully tool such as lens reads these states, and model compression, which distils smaller or pruned student by matching the intermediate states of its teacher, relies on what these states mean (Romero et al., 2015; Dasgupta and Cohn, 2025; Muralidharan et al., 2024). This meaning is set by the remaining layers, which read each state in the context of its prefix. Two families of methods address these states and fail in opposite ways. The first reads state with lens: the logit lens applies the output frame to every layer unchanged (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens learns one affine map per layer fitted to the models output (Belrose et al., 2023), and the Jacobian lens averages the Jacobian of the remaining layers over positions and prompts (Gurnee et al., 2026). Each fixes one linear map per layer, so every state of layer is read identically, regardless of its prefix. The second family keeps every state and does without reading. It treats the states of layer as point cloud and reports its rank, intrinsic dimension, anisotropy or similarity to other layers (Kornblith et al., 2019; Ansuini et al., 2019; Garrido et al., 2022; Skean et al., 2025). Such statistics describe how the states are distributed rather than how the model uses them: two states close in the cloud may lead to different predictions, and two distant ones to the same. Both families omit the frame in which the model itself reads state: the directions along which state changes the logit of token are property of the remaining layers and therefore differ from Figure 1: Angle between the lexical readout of LEXFRAME[] for token (grey) and the direction each method offers, after every fourth layer of OLMo3-7B: medians over states and tokens, zero at the output by definition. layer to layer; because these layers attend to the preceding tokens, they also differ between contexts, so no method with one map per layer can follow them, however it is fitted. In OLMo3-7B (Figure 1), after layer 16 of 32, the logit-lens direction for token deviates by 75 degrees from the models own lexical readout and the Jacobian-lens direction by 77 degrees, and four layers before the output both still deviate by at least 40 degrees. Our starting point is that these directions, the lexical readouts, form reference frame: we call their family at state its lexical reference frame, and the frame that the complete model induces its native frame. The native frame returns the models output at every layer, so useful frame withholds stated part of this computation: the frame of order n, written LEXFRAME[n], transports state through the models own layers with rounds of attention between positions and replaces the remaining attention by typical attention output, estimated once per layer from unlabelled text. LEXFRAME[0] reads what state holds by itself, LEXFRAME[1] what it draws from its prefix, and LEXFRAME[] is the native frame. The idea is simple: read state the way the model reads it, through the layers that remain and with the context it sees. lens ignores the context and is therefore bounded; frame uses it, as far as its order allows. As nothing is fitted to the models output, lexical reference frames are comparable across layers, checkpoints and models. We evaluate lexical reference frames at every layer of SmolLM3-3B (Hugging Face, 2025) and OLMo3-7B (Team OLMo, 2025) and at 16 of their training checkpoints, against the logit lens, the Jacobian lens, supervised probe and distances on the point cloud. From the middle layers on, LEXFRAME[1] recovers the native frames lexical readouts beyond the bound of every lens and matches the models output in content and confidence, which lenses do only near the output; one round of attention to the prefix closes most of the gap that LEXFRAME[0] leaves. Its readings settle on the models prediction early enough for an early exit to skip more than two fifths of the layers, and they stay faithful along training while the logit lens degrades. Distances on the point cloud barely predict the effect of replacing state, as lexical readouts lie almost entirely outside the directions in which the states vary. In the coordinates of the frame, the lexical basis writes prediction into the stream more selectively than the readout, and differences of coefficients attribute it to layers and sublayers more faithfully than attribution patching. We therefore expect lexical reference frames to be strong alternative to lenses in these applications. In summary, this paper makes three contributions. We show that the layers that remain give every hidden state its own frame in the vocabulary, and we prove that no lens with one map per layer can follow this frame across the different contexts in which state occurs. We define frames that read hidden state in the models native semantics through its own layers with chosen amount of context, and we compute them in closed form from unlabelled text, without any training. We show on two model families and their training checkpoints that these frames follow the model from the middle layers on, where lenses fail, and support early exit, steering and attribution at every layer of the model.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Prior work on the intermediate layers of language models asks which tokens state stands for, how the states of layer are distributed, and which directions or components drive prediction, and reference frame bears on all three questions. Language model lenses. The logit lens reads an intermediate state with the models own output frame (nostalgebraist, 2020), and it underlies studies of how predictions are refined across depth (Jastrzebski et al., 2017; Geva et al., 2020, 2022; Dar et al., 2022; Halawi et al., 2023; Katz et al., 2024; Wendler et al., 2024; Lad et al., 2024). Later lenses use map per layer, trained to match the output (Belrose et al., 2023; Din et al., 2023) or given by Jacobian of the remaining layers (Hernandez et al., 2023; Gurnee et al., 2026), or patch the state into another forward pass (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Pal et al., 2023). Gu et al. (2026c) fix set of anchors and measure the states of all layers against them, and Gu et al. (2026b) tie the input and output frames to each other through the pseudo-inverse of one shared token memory. Lenses are thus frames that ignore the context, and we bound how closely any can approximate the native frame. Point clouds and manifolds. large body of work summarises the states of layer by statistics of the cloud they form, such as similarity between layers (Raghu et al., 2017; Kornblith et al., 2019), intrinsic dimension (Facco et al., 2018; Ansuini et al., 2019; Valeriani et al., 2023), effective rank (Garrido et al., 2022) and anisotropy (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Razzhigaev et al., 2023; Bernas et al., 2026). Recent studies follow these statistics across layers (Cheng et al., 2024; Skean et al., 2025) and across training (Saphra and Lopez, 2018; Tigges et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024). We quantify how much these statistics reveal about the way the model uses the states of layer. Directions and components. Linear probes learn direction from labelled states (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Tenney et al., 2019; Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2021), and steering methods add direction to the states to change the output (Subramani et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024). Both rest on the hypothesis that concepts are represented as directions (Park et al., 2023), which Park et al. (2026) derive from the information geometry of the softmax for the output layer only. The contribution of component to prediction is likewise computed along direction, by projecting what the component writes onto the output frame (Wang et al., 2022), or measured by patching (Meng et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023; Syed et al., 2023). frame supplies directions for each state without supervision, and we test them in steering and attribution at every layer.

sections.title: 3 Lexical Reference Frames
sections.content: We describe hidden state by the frame in which the model reads it in its vocabulary: fixed at both ends of the residual stream, adaptive in between and approximated at finite order (Appendix C). 3.1 Preliminaries Layers are numbered from 1 to L, and layer 0 denotes the embedding. Let xℓ(t) Rd be the hidden state, the residual stream after layer ℓ at position t. Layer reads the stream and writes its update back into it (Elhage et al., 2021; Veit et al., 2016), (cid:0)xk1(t), ak(t)(cid:1), where ak(t) is the xk(t) = Fk output of its attention at position t, which depends on the states of the other positions, and Fk contains the residual connections, the normalisations and the feed-forward block. The native semantics of the model are its vocabulary labels, the smallest units of meaning that it receives and produces, in which reference frame expresses state. (cid:80) At its two interfaces the model itself gives every label geometric form. At the input, the embedding assigns label the state Ev. At the output, the logit of is zv = N (xL(t)) with the final normalisation and the unembedding row wv, and its centred value is cv = zv 1 zu. The state whose logits come closest, in least squares, to the indicator ev of is sv = +ev, which Gu et al. (2024) call its semantic basis. We call such family of vectors, one per label, lexical basis. The input lexical basis and the output lexical basis are the same for every text, so the reference frames that they span, the input frame and the output frame, are fixed. Earlier work measures states against these fixed frames and decomposes them into coefficients on the output lexical basis, to select layers for finetuning (Gu et al., 2025) and to transfer knowledge across model scales (Gu et al., 2026a). 3.2 Native Reference Frame Between the interfaces the model defines no basis, and frame must be adaptive: specific to the layer 3 Figure 2: Lexical bases of five tokens (colours) and one state (black) across the layers: fixed at the two interfaces (filled), dependent on the context in between (hollow). and sensitive to the context. state receives its meaning from the layers that remain, which read it from the stream. They transport xℓ(t), together with the states of its prefix, to the last layer, where the output frame applies. We call this passage layerwise transport and write Tℓ for the map from xℓ(t) to xL(t) with the states of the prefix held fixed. The lexical basis at the layer is sℓ(v) = + ℓ sv, the direction in which the state must move for the output to move along sv. Both are determined anew for every state, as Figure 2 illustrates: they depend on the layer, since Jℓ contains all remaining layers, and on the context, since these layers attend to the prefix. The frame that the complete model induces is the native reference frame of the state, in short its native frame. Basis and coefficients give the stream coordinates in the vocabulary at every layer, which is the purpose of the frame: the coefficients read the stream, the basis writes into it, and their differences attribute prediction to what layer writes. The native frame is the reference for interventions, but its reading is the models output; an informative reading withholds part of the remaining computation. 3.3 Orders of Reference Frames ℓ frame of order replaces the transport Tℓ by one that computes only rounds of attention between positions, and so has its own lexical readouts, lexical basis and reading q(n) . Its transport still runs through every remaining layer, which makes it specific to the layer; from order 1 on the state also attends to its prefix, and the order counts the hops that information may travel between positions above layer ℓ. frame that withholds more is further from the model but more informative about the state, and as nothing in it is fitted to the models output, agreement with the model is finding. As Figure 3 shows, every remaining layer updates the state at position from the state one layer below and its attention over the other positions; all frames keep the first input and differ in the second. Order 0. LEXFRAME[0] withholds the prefix and reads state without its context, and its reading is what the state holds by itself. It transports xℓ(t) through the layers > ℓ with the models own Fk, and it replaces the attention output by typical one, ˆak(u) = ak + (u uk) Gk, (3) 4 Figure 3: What frame of each order computes to read the state at position of layer ℓ: the layers own attention (solid black) and typical attention outputs (dashed blue). The order in brackets counts the rounds of attention between positions above layer ℓ, like hops of message passing: the context reaches the state only through the state itself (0), directly from the prefix (1), through one relay in the prefix (2), or without limit (). where is the attention input at position t, uk and ak are the means of the attention input and output of layer k, and Gk is the ridge regression of the attention output on its input, fitted once for each layer on unlabelled calibration text. Because the transport keeps every remaining layer, LEXFRAME[0] is still nonlinear reading that depends on the state, unlike lens, and it lacks only what the remaining layers would gather from other positions. Order 1. LEXFRAME[1] lets the state attend to its prefix. The state at position is transported as before, but in every layer its attention is the layers own attention, computed over the prefix. The states of the prefix are themselves transported from layer ℓ by LEXFRAME[0], so the frame withholds only the attention among the prefix positions after layer ℓ. The state attends with the layers own queries, keys and values, but each prefix position evolves in isolation. The reading is what the state draws from its prefix; the step from LEXFRAME[0] measures what this one round of attention contributes. In LEXFRAME[2] Order 2. the attention also reaches within the prefix: the prefix positions attend too, each with the layers own attention over its own prefix, which is transported by LEXFRAME[0]. Information can therefore travel two steps, from an earlier token through prefix position to the state, route that LEXFRAME[1] cannot represent. The step from LEXFRAME[1] to LEXFRAME[2] measures what this one exchange among the prefix positions contributes. In general LEXFRAME[n] attends to prefix of states of order 1; each order thus computes one more round of attention between positions, and reading at order runs + 1 streams through the remaining layers. Higher orders add exchanges within the prefix and converge to the model. Order . In the limit of the order nothing is withheld, and LEXFRAME[] recovers the model as the native frame: every position attends to the true states of its prefix, which are the states that the model itself computes. Two identities follow: the reading of every layer in LEXFRAME[] equals the models output, and LEXFRAME[n] is exact wherever at most layers remain. Near the output all orders therefore agree with the model; they differ where much of the computation lies ahead. The reading of LEXFRAME[] adds nothing to the models prediction; its value lies in its lexical readouts and basis, which every frame of finite order approximates.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We compare frames with lenses and point clouds, then test their coordinates and their use in steering and attribution. Appendix details the setup; Appendix adds training checkpoints, lexical readouts, context length, settling depth and ablations. Setup. We use SmolLM3-3B with 36 layers and OLMo3-7B with 32 layers, recent competitive open-weight models that release checkpoints from every stage of training; SmolLM3 ties its input 5 Figure 4: Divergence in nats from the models output to the reading of each frame and each lens, per layer: each further order lowers it at nearly every layer, while both lenses stay several nats above all frames until near the output. and output embeddings, OLMo3 does not. We run them in the precision of the released weights and report pairs of values in this order. Text comes from WikiText-103, cut into sequences of 128 tokens. The typical attention outputs are estimated on 256 sequences of the training split, and every measurement uses the test split and every layer. The Jacobian lens is fitted with its reference implementation on 100 prompts. We omit the tuned lens, which is trained on the models output, the quantity on which readings are scored, and is bounded like every lens. As supervised reference we add linear probe, ridge regression of the centred logit on the states, fitted on separate text. Divergences are KullbackLeibler divergences from the models output to reading, in nats, and averages over layers are unweighted. LEXFRAME[] is the reference for readings and the exact frame in interventions. 4.1 Comparison with Lenses We compare frames and lenses in the directions along which they measure label and in the distributions that they assign to state. At intermediate layers, LEXFRAME[] departs sharply from the output frame: at mid-depth its lexical readouts have cosine of only 0.07 and 0.26 with those of the last layer, and their coherence across contexts is 0.09 and 0.12. We compare each methods direction for label, the gradient of its reading or its fixed vector, with these readouts for 64 labels across the frequency ranking. LEXFRAME[1] follows them closely from the middle layers on, with layer-averaged cosine of 0.89 and 0.87, because it computes the same transport and withholds only the attention among the prefix positions. The lenses and the probe average between 0.21 and 0.36, and their failure is structural rather than matter of fitting. κℓ The Jacobian lens stays at or below the bound at every layer and the supervised probe falls further below it, whereas at mid-depth, where the bound is 0.30 and 0.35, LEXFRAME[1] reaches 0.97 and 0.97: no single direction matches readout that changes with the context. LEXFRAME[2] raises the mean cosine to 0.95 and 0.95: LEXFRAME[1] misses the exchange within the prefix. The divergence from the models output (Figure 4) shows the same ladder: averaged over layers, LEXFRAME[0] is at 0.87 and 0.93 nats, LEXFRAME[1] at 0.16 and 0.15, and LEXFRAME[2] at 0.06 and 0.05. The gap is widest in SmolLM3, whose output frame is also its input frame: at the embedding its logit lens names the input token itself for 0.83 of the positions, against 0.00 in OLMo3. Conversely, layer skip, which feeds layers states to the last four layers with attention but without transport, remains at 7.00 and 2.59 nats: reading needs both transport and attention. Since lexical readout is the gradient of logit, moving along the 7 directions in which the cloud varies changes the logits far less than moving as far along the readout: the cloud mainly describes variation that the remaining layers ignore, yet distances weigh it fully. 4.3 Coordinates at Intermediate Layers At the output, the vocabulary is coordinate system for the residual stream: the lexical basis gives the axes, the directions in which writing label moves state, and the coefficients give the coordinates, how much of each label the state holds. Table 4: Coefficients on the output lexical basis against model logits on 512 positions, averaged over layers: divergence (nats) at the best scale, top-token agreement. 4.4 Steering and Attribution The two halves of these coordinates serve two interventions on the stream: steering writes into it along the basis, and attribution reads through the coefficients what component wrote. In steering, the task is to make the runner-up token u, the target that needs the smallest move, overtake the top token by moving single state. frame offers two directions for this: the lexical readout of the logit difference, bℓ(u) bℓ(v), which is its gradient, and the difference of the lexical basis vectors, sℓ(u) sℓ(v). We move each state along each direction in steps from 0.01 to 1 times its norm and record the first step that flips the prediction and the change in the other tokens at that step. Along the lexical readout, LEXFRAME[1] flips 0.92 and 0.94 of the predictions, nearly as many as LEXFRAME[] with 0.95 and 0.97, and the lenses at most 0.81. The lexical basis flips nearly as many, but it disturbs the other tokens far less, 0.009 and 0.004 nats at the flip against 0.033 and 0.025, and therefore makes the most clean flips, 0.73 and 0.85 of the predictions. As in the lexical-basis test, the readout is the steepest ascent of the logit difference and spreads the change over every token moving with or v, while the basis is the move whose firstorder effect on the output comes closest to raising against alone. Jacobian of LEXFRAME[1] reaches 0.71 and 0.82; selective steering thus works even without access to the Jacobian of the model itself. At single positions of layer 16, the readout of LEXFRAME[1] flips the prediction with median step of 0.10 and 0.03 of the states norm, as for LEXFRAME[], while both lenses need steps ten times as large. In attribution, the task is to quantify how much component, layer or one of its two sublayers, contributed to the centred logit of the predicted token. As the reference we remove what the component wrote at one position, leave the prefix untouched, complete the forward pass, and measure the change in the logit, on 64 sequences. This effect is the difference of coefficients in LEXFRAME[], so the test asks whether frame that withholds exchanges within the prefix still attributes as the model does. In frame, the attribution is the change in the coefficient of the predicted token when the component is removed from the state. We compare it with the same difference taken in the two lenses, of which the logit lens gives direct logit attribution, and with linear attributions, the inner product of lexical readout with the component, which for LEXFRAME[] is attribution patching (Syed et al., 2023; Kramár et al., 2024). The agreement holds at single positions: across their layers, the difference correlates with the measured effect at 0.97 and 0.93 in the median and exceeds both lenses at 0.99 and 0.98 of positions. linear attribution assumes that the effect of write is proportional to it, and its deficit is largest for the feed-forward block (MLP), 0.88 and 0.90 against 0.63 and 0.71, but small for attention, 0.79 and 0.85 against 0.75 and 0.84: the remaining layers respond almost linearly to attention writes and far beyond first order to feed-forward writes. The two lenses reach at most 0.20: direct logit attribution measures only the direct path from write to the output, which carries little of the effect.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Every hidden state of language model has native reference frame, fixed at the two ends of the residual stream and adaptive in between, and lexical reference frames approximate it to stated order without fitting to the models output. In two model families LEXFRAME[1] recovers the models lexical readouts and output from mid-depth on, beyond the reach of any method with one map per layer, and it attributes and steers predictions. The frame explains why fixed lens fails at mid-depth, increasingly so along training, and why the point cloud reveals little about how the model uses state. To interpret state, read it as the model does: through the layers that remain, with the context it sees, and in its own native semantics, reading that can stand in for lenses.

sections.title: A Technical Details
sections.content: A.1 Implementation Details Aaquib Syed, Can Rager, and Arthur Conmy. 2023. Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated CirPreprint, arXiv:2310.10348. cuit Discovery. ArXiv:2310.10348. Models and data. The SmolLM3 checkpoints follow grid in which the number of training tokens roughly triples from one checkpoint to the 12 next, and the OLMo3 checkpoints are chosen at matching token counts, with the randomly initialised model and an early checkpoint at four billion tokens in addition. Both families include the checkpoints at the end of their later training stages. The Jacobian lens is defined from layer 1 on, and every average over layers runs over layers 1 to L1, without the embedding, where the Jacobian lens is undefined, and the output, where every reading is exact. We calibrate on 256 sequences of 128 tokens from the training split and evaluate on 64 sequences of 128 tokens from the test split. Estimation methods. The frames involve no training: the typical attention outputs are fitted in closed form from one forward pass over the calibration text, with the ridge of every layer chosen from fixed grid by two-fold cross-validation over the calibration sequences. Gradients are taken through the released weights in their stored half precision. The lexical basis sℓ(v) = + ℓ sv solves minδJℓδ sv2 + λδ2 with λ = 103 ℓ sv2/sv2, the same relative ridge in both experiments that use it. In the lexical-basis test we form Jℓ explicitly in 32bit arithmetic, with the stored weights cast exactly, and solve the problem in closed form for all labels at once; every move is then evaluated in the model itself, whichever Jacobian produced the direction. In steering, which needs the basis at every position, we solve the problem without forming Jℓ by 30 steps of LSMR (Fong and Saunders, 2011) from zero, where product Jℓδ is one forward-mode pass and product ℓ one backward pass. Evaluation methods. Positions and tokens are sampled once with fixed seeds, every experiment uses the same test sequences, and all results are from single run, which is deterministic up to the rounding of the arithmetic. The first identity of Section 3.3 holds up to the rounding of half precision, with divergence of 0.0009 and 0.0002 nats. The calibration error is the expected calibration error of Guo et al. (2017) with 15 bins. The substitution test was repeated on second, disjoint part of the test split, where it gives 0.94 and 0.95 for LEXFRAME[1] and 0.28 and 0.27 for the cosine distance, nearly the same as on the first. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from at least 300 resamples of the test sequences, so that positions of the same sequence stay together. They appear as bands in the figures; in Tables 1 to 7, which report means, their half-width is at most 12% of divergence, 0.004 nats for the change in the other tokens in steering, and 0.04 for every other value. A.2 Artifacts and Computations We use SmolLM3-3B (Hugging Face, 2025) and OLMo3-7B (Team OLMo, 2025) with their published intermediate checkpoints, both released under the Apache 2.0 licence. The text is the English WikiText-103 corpus (Merity et al., 2016), released under the Creative Commons AttributionShareAlike licence, with about 103 million tokens in its training split and 0.25 million in its test split. Our use of these artifacts is consistent with their intended use, and the text contains no information that we collected or annotated. The experiments ran on NVIDIA RTX 4080 SUPER GPUs, and every run uses single GPU. The whole project used about 500 GPU hours, of which about 100 hours produced the final experiments reported in this paper; the remainder was spent on preliminary experiments. The implementation is written in Python 3.12 with PyTorch 2.12 and Transformers 5.16. A.3 AI Use Disclosure AI assistants supported the writing of this paper and the preparation of its code. The authors checked all text, code and results and take full responsibility.

sections.content: Training checkpoints. LEXFRAME[] is defined through the layers that remain, so it changes with the layer and whenever these layers change. Figure 6 shows this for every label of the direction test, as the cosine between the lexical readout of LEXFRAME[] at layer and at the last layer of the same forward pass. In the base models the middepth cosine is 0.07 and 0.26: the output frame is far from the frame that the model uses there. This departure is learned: at the first checkpoint the middepth cosine is 0.34 in SmolLM3, whose earliest released checkpoint is already well into training, and 0.71 in the randomly initialised OLMo3, and it falls over the course of training. frame that does not adapt suits only the last layers, where this cosine stays high at every checkpoint. Across checkpoints, the ranking of the readings is stable in both families. In SmolLM3 the divergence of the logit lens from the models output grows from 4.82 to 29.06 nats, while that of LEXFRAME[1] only moves from 0.15 to 0.16. The decline of the logit lens thus follows the rotation of the frame at mid-depth: lens degrades not because 13 of the exchange among prefix positions still lies ahead: there LEXFRAME[1] reaches 0.33 and 0.18, and LEXFRAME[2], which adds one such exchange, already reaches 0.56 and 0.44. Figure 6: Cosine between the lexical readouts of LEXFRAME[] at layer and at the last layer, for every checkpoint from the first (lightest) to the last (darkest). the model becomes harder to read but because the models own frames move away from the output frame. Averaged over layers, LEXFRAME[1] agrees with the models top token on at least 0.85 and 0.86 of the states at every trained checkpoint, while the logit lens falls from 0.21 to 0.04 and from 0.27 to 0.15. Every value is an average over all layers and over the same 64 test sequences, and the typical attention outputs are estimated anew at every checkpoint, so the comparison along training is free of the confound that lens fitted at one checkpoint is stale at the next. The randomly initialised OLMo3 is control: LEXFRAME[1] is within 0.11 nats of its output and the logit lens 0.52 nats away, as every frame is built from its models layers. Lexical readouts. Figure 7 resolves the comparison of lexical readouts by layer. LEXFRAME[1] exceeds cosine of 0.95 with LEXFRAME[] from layer 16 and 15 on, and LEXFRAME[2] from layer 10 and 9 on, while the fixed directions approach the frame only in the last layers, where little computation remains. At mid-depth the Jacobian lens reaches only 0.20 and 0.23, so even lens fitted to the models own Jacobian stays well below κℓ, and it does not exceed it at any the bound layer. The bound itself rises toward the output, as the readouts depend less and less on the context, and every fixed direction rises with it. The frames are weakest at the first layers, where most Figure 7: Cosine of each methods direction for label with the lexical readout of LEXFRAME[], per layer, and the coherence bound κℓ. Context length. longer context offers more positions to attend to and therefore more attention that frame of finite order withholds, so long sequences test the orders directly. We repeated the readings on 64 sequences of 1024 tokens, with the typical attention outputs estimated on the same number of calibration tokens. The divergence of LEXFRAME[1] from the models output rises only from 0.16 and 0.15 to 0.25 and 0.18 nats; the order of all methods is unchanged, with LEXFRAME[0] at 1.11 and 1.06, LEXFRAME[2] at 0.15 and 0.08 and the lenses at 6.04 or more, and LEXFRAME[1] still agrees with the models top token on 0.84 and 0.86 of the states. The attention among the prefix positions that LEXFRAME[1] withholds grows with the context, but at intermediate layers it contributes little to what state means to the model, so longer prefix adds little to the divergence. Figure 8 resolves the divergence by position, that is, by the length of the context: it grows slowly, without break between the two lengths, so the frame does not degrade at any particular context length. LEXFRAME[] and the correlation of its attribution with the measured effect drop markedly. The attention that frame withholds is therefore not constant: it varies with the input of the attention, and one linear map per layer already captures enough of this variation to keep the frame close to the model. With four calibration sequences, about five hundred tokens, the divergence of LEXFRAME[1] from the models output is 0.41 and 0.34 nats, against 0.16 and 0.15 with the 256 sequences used throughout. The estimate needs little text because it has few degrees of freedom: one linear map per layer between two quantities inside that layer, with ridge chosen by cross-validation. On three disjoint calibration texts, the divergence lies between 0.160 and 0.163 nats in SmolLM3 and between 0.146 and 0.151 in OLMo3, so the frame barely depends on the choice of calibration text. Counted back from the last layer, the unbroken run of layers whose reading names the models top token shows from which depth prediction is settled, the quantity on which early exit relies. Over all 8128 positions and every layer  (Table 7)  , LEXFRAME[1] is settled over 0.82 and 0.81 of the layers, the Jacobian lens over 0.09 and 0.09 and the logit lens over 0.03 and 0.11, and each order lengthens the run, from 0.58 and 0.58 for LEXFRAME[0] to 0.89 and 0.90 for LEXFRAME[2]. sections.title: D Discussion
sections.content: The framework rests on one idea: read hidden state as the model reads it, through the layers that remain and with the context it sees. Lenses read each layer with one fixed map, and point clouds read no state at all; frame lets the remaining layers, which decide what state means, do the reading in the models native semantics, its vocabulary. reference frame separates two questions that lens answers at once: along which directions the model measures label at state, and how much of the label the state holds. Existing methods appear as special cases: lens is frame that does not adapt to the context and is therefore bounded by the coherence of the native frame, probe is fixed lexical readout learned under supervision, and point cloud is set of states without frame. The native frame answers both questions exactly, and the orders make it informative by stating what is withheld. Both parts of the models reading are necessary: transport alone, in LEXFRAME[0], already brings reading far closer to the model than any fitted map, whereas attention to the prefix without transport, in layer skip, does not, and no fitting lifts method that ignores the context above the coherence bound. The order thus makes the use of the context controlled variable, so that what each hop between positions contributes can be measured. The value of this view lies in what it makes comparable. The vocabulary is shared by every layer, checkpoint and model of family, and frame expresses all of their states in it without trained component whose faithfulness would need separate argument. The native frame is thus reference against which any interpretation of hidden state can be scored, and frame calibrated anew in single pass can follow model through training, fine-tuning or editing in the same units. Early exit, hallucination detection and knowledge editing read hidden states through lenses or probes, and model compression matches the hidden states of teacher, so each could read these states in the frame of the model instead; we expect such uses to benefit, but leave them to future work. therefore exceed (cid:112)κℓ(v) on average: the bound is property of LEXFRAME[] and not of an estimator. lens followed by the final normalisation varies with the state only through , and in practice it also stays below this bound. Write hn (t) for the state of position at layer > ℓ in LEXFRAME[n]. Order 0 replaces the attention of every layer by the typical attention output, and order 1 computes the layers own attention over the prefix states of order 1, hn (t) = Fk an (t) = Attk (cid:0)hn k1(t), an (cid:0)hn (t)(cid:1), k1(t); {hn1 k1(s)}s<t (6) (cid:1), with hn ℓ = xℓ for every n. By induction on n, the state of order equals the true state for its first layers: hn (t) = xk(t) for ℓ + n. This holds trivially for = 0, and if it holds for 1, the attention of layer ℓ + attends to prefix states of order 1 at layer 1 ℓ + 1, which are the true ones. Two identities follow. LEXFRAME[n] is exact wherever at most layers remain, ℓ n, and for ℓ every state is the true one, so LEXFRAME[] returns the models output at every layer. The orders differ from the model only through the attention between positions more than layers above the state. C.3 Complexity Analysis We count costs in forward passes, measure independent of the hardware. Calibration is one forward pass over the calibration text and one ridge regression per layer. Reading the states of layer ℓ at order runs + 1 streams through the ℓ remaining layers, so reading every layer of sequence, at all positions at once, costs about (n + 1)(L + 1)/2 forward passes. fitted lens reads state with one matrix product, which is cheaper per state, but the fit is not: the Jacobian lens needs the Jacobian of the last state with respect to the states of every layer, one backward pass per dimension of the state, for each of its prompts, about backward passes in total. With LEXFRAME[1], lens therefore becomes cheaper only after about d/(L + 1) sequences have been read at every layer, and the fit must be repeated for every checkpoint, while frame only repeats its calibration pass. Fitting the Jacobian lens took 18 and 44 times as long as calibrating the frames and reading every layer of the 64 test sequences at orders 0 to 2.
